Task 1: As-built invoice approval diagrams

This assessment describes the current implementation, based on the application source inspected on 24 October 2026 and AGENTS.md. The diagrams were generated and validated using Mermaid MCP. Evidence identifiers link each diagram element to its supporting source. The planned deployment described in ops/ is excluded from the current-state assessment. Application code was not changed.

Scope: the browser UI and one ASP.NET Core application. The domain library, invoice repository and session store run within the server process. These are logical runtime boundaries; no production deployment topology is asserted.

1. As-built container view

The ASP.NET Core application serves the HTML, CSS and JavaScript interface and exposes the invoice API. The browser calls this API on the same origin. Successful login returns an opaque session token, which the browser includes in subsequent API requests. The server resolves the token against its in-memory session store. Invoice records are also stored in memory.

The code has no database, message broker/topic, payment provider or external identity provider in this runtime path. Server internals are listed inside the server box so they are not mistaken for separately deployed services.

2. Invoice approval sequence: success and failure

The sequence traces one approval request, including authentication, authorization, invoice validation, state mutation and response handling. Server lifelines represent components or framework stages within the same application, rather than separate deployed services.

The sequence starts when a user clicks Approve. It follows the /approve action, not the separate Reject action. Login and submission are outside the sequence; seeded invoices can already be pending. The server first checks identity, then role, then whether the invoice exists and is pending. Only after all checks pass does it mark the invoice Approved and record the signed-in username and UTC time. The UI then reloads the invoice list and removes this invoice from the pending display through its local filter.

OutcomeMeaning
401The token is absent or unknown. With a local session, the browser signs out and returns to the login view.
403The session exists, but its role is neither Approver nor Admin. The role filter stops the action.
404No invoice matches this ID.
409The invoice exists but is not PendingApproval. Draft, Approved and Rejected invoices cannot be approved through this rule.
200The approval succeeded and the updated invoice is returned.

Agent inferences and modeling choices

  1. I1: Runtime grouping. The two-container interpretation and logical system boundary are architectural modeling choices based on browser JavaScript, same-origin fetch calls, the API project's Domain reference and Program.cs registrations. They do not assert a production host topology, Docker deployment or number of deployed replicas.
  2. I2: Restart behavior. Because invoices and sessions are singleton in-process collections with no persistence in the inspected implementation, restarting the application is expected to recreate seeded invoices and discard existing sessions. This is a code-based consequence, not a restart experiment performed for this task.
  3. I3: Sequence presentation. MVC and ApprovalsController share a lifeline; the role filter runs before the action. Response arrows omit framework unwinding. The follow-up GET is summarized in a note to keep the diagram focused on approval. These are presentation abstractions, not extra calls or services.
  4. I4: Single-request scope. The diagram follows one approval request without concurrent mutations. It does not establish transaction or concurrency guarantees across the separate lookup, mutation and update operations.

Verification findings and corrections

  • Kept the domain project and both memory stores inside the API runtime; no separate database or external service was inferred from the planned deployment in ops/.
  • Verified middleware ordering: static files are served before authentication; login is exempt from the API session check. “Every endpoint is behind sign-in” in AGENTS.md is a convention, not a literal description of login or static-file behavior. Evidence: Program.cs; InvokeAsync.
  • Corrected the entry-state wording: submission is not always required because the repository seeds pending invoices. Evidence: _invoices; Submit.
  • Verified that the approver name comes from the server session, not the request body. Evidence: Approve.
  • Included the actual 401, 403, 404 and 409 branches. The configured demo users both have allowed approval roles, so 403 is an implemented guard branch rather than an expected outcome with either supplied demo account. Evidence: Users; OnActionExecuting.
  • Did not add a 400 business-rule branch to Approve: its implementation calls Find and EnsurePending. The missing-reason ArgumentException belongs to Reject, and Handle maps that exception to 400. Reject is a separate action and is not an approval failure. Evidence: Approve / Reject; Handle.
  • Corrected the 403 label to avoid asserting a response-body format that the role filter itself does not supply. The 401 middleware explicitly sets a status and returns without writing a body. Evidence: Auth/RequireRoleAttribute.cs; Auth/SessionAuthMiddleware.cs.
  • Verified the UI fetches all invoices and filters pending invoices locally. It does not use a dedicated pending-approval endpoint. Evidence: refresh.
  • Verified that refresh errors are caught in decide even after the approval succeeds. Such an error does not undo approval. A 401 sign-out hides the app view, so the decision-error element is not necessarily visible. Evidence: decide / signOut / render; wwwroot/index.html.
  • Both final diagram sources passed Mermaid rendering after sequence-message syntax corrections. The generation review recorded a visual check of label readability and branch nesting.

Validation was a static source trace plus Mermaid parsing/rendering and visual inspection. Existing ApprovalServiceTests corroborate success, Draft rejection and missing-invoice behavior; tests were initially inspected and were subsequently executed as part of Task 1: the final suite passed all eight tests, including the new architecture test. See the execution evidence. No end-to-end or deployed API test coverage is claimed. Framework routing errors, arbitrary malformed requests and infrastructure failures are outside this business-path diagram.

Current-state limitations

The repository returns mutable invoice objects. ApprovalService changes those objects outside the repository lock before calling Update. The lock therefore does not make the complete lookup, validation and mutation sequence atomic. The diagrams describe a single request and do not claim protection against simultaneous decisions.

Approval records the latest decision on the invoice; this flow does not establish a durable, seven-year approval audit history or delivery to PayEx. These are target-state requirements.
